column3: It repeats the full sequence of punishment arriving, humiliating its recipient, and then becoming abiding.
The branch resonance is not localized to this verse and does not clarify punishment, humiliation, or endurance.
Its blessed lasting abode helps frame muqim as a settled condition, though it is a contrary destination.
It closely repeats the warning that humiliation-bringing punishment will come, within a contested prophetic address.
The immediately preceding surah context names God's might and vengeance, supporting the warning's authority without its full sequence.
Its ritual destination and conditional punishment do not illuminate the focal punishment becoming a lasting condition.
It directly names an abiding punishment and the impossibility of leaving the Fire.
The arrival of divine might produces a confession of wrongdoing, supplying a judgment-arrival frame.
It explicitly treats entry into the Fire as humiliation and denies wrongdoers any helper.
It directly combines enduring residence in Hell with an abiding punishment.
As the immediately prior verse, it supplies the warning that each side's position will soon be tested by outcome.
It explicitly promises humiliation for disbelievers, though it does not describe the abiding punishment.
Wrath settling upon a person and causing ruin closely parallels punishment coming to rest upon its recipient.
Universal questioning supplies only a general accountability horizon for the announced punishment.
Standing in a mosque and purification do not clarify the focal warning.
Its fixed road shares only the settled sense of muqim, in a different setting.
It directly supplies the same-surah pattern of punishment arriving unexpectedly after denial.
Repeatedly turning from signs only broadly precedes the punishment arrival in the focus.
It combines abasement before the Fire with an abiding punishment for wrongdoers.
The unrelated channel resonance does not add to the focus's punishment sequence.
Its challenge to produce proof for false gods gives only a remote background for later judgment.
The inviolability of revelation does not clarify punishment, humiliation, or permanence.
God's exclusive sovereignty and the return to Him give the local judgment frame behind the warning.
A known assigned station does not illuminate punishment settling upon a person.
It explicitly locates humiliation on the Day of Resurrection and exposes the failure of alleged partners.
The branch resonance is not localized and this narrative episode does not clarify the focus.
Fear of the Lord's station supplies only a broad contrary accountability frame.
What comes upon an object reduces it to ruin, supporting the destructive force of the focal arrival.
Exclusive worship in the opening does not by itself clarify the punishment formula.
It mentions humiliating the defiantly disobedient, but in a distinct historical action.
Divine punishment and humiliation are joined, though no enduring condition is stated.
The general instructive status of narratives does not clarify the focus's stated consequence.
It explicitly calls enduring residence in Hell the great humiliation.
The prophetic legal and ethical description does not add to the warning's consequence.
The same-surah scene of just judgment provides the final setting in which the warning is realized.
The prayer not to be humiliated at resurrection directly names the adverse outcome avoided in the focus.
An offer of strength to bring a throne does not clarify divine punishment arriving.
Provision and replacement are not connected to the focal punishment sequence.
The demand that alleged partners be brought only faintly echoes the focus's coming language.
The legal status of a city does not clarify punishment, humiliation, or enduring residence.
The same-surah repudiation of false sonship and assertion of God's dominion gives a broad polemical setting for judgment.
The introduction to Moses' account does not clarify the focus.
Rules about permitted food and hunting do not illuminate the announced punishment.
A condition for receiving grain does not clarify punishment arriving or settling.
Guidance after descent and freedom from fear do not address the focal consequence.
The prayer not to be humiliated on the Day of Resurrection directly parallels the focus's humiliation.
The same-surah conclusion portrays judgment decided in truth, supplying the setting of final consequences.
It explicitly contrasts receiving guidance with punishment coming face to face.
It directly names a punishment that arrives and remains settled.
The Fire enclosing wrongdoers supplies a durable punitive environment, though not the humiliation formula.
The sacred house as a secure place does not clarify the focal punishment.
Death comes from every direction and is followed by severe punishment, intensifying inevitable punitive arrival.
The same-surah dispute over intermediaries is placed under God's judgment, supplying background for the warning.
Human attempts to turn believers away do not clarify the punishment announced here.
It directly joins enduring residence in the Fire with a humiliating punishment.
Divine guidance and misguidance give only a broad authority frame for the consequence.
Different directions and gathering do not clarify punishment or humiliation.
Following the rebellious one is said to lead to the punishment of the Blaze.
The same-surah appeal to the Creator as judge supplies the adjudicative horizon of the warning.
It explicitly joins worldly humiliation with a later burning punishment for one who turns others astray.
God's power to punish or show mercy and the return to Him provides the broader judgment alternative.
The mission to bring a people from darkness to light does not clarify the focal punishment.
Demanding a sign to come offers only a remote parallel to the focus's coming punishment.
It directly assigns disbelievers the punishment of the Fire, though without humiliation or duration.
The same-surah account of death being retained or released supports divine control over the persons judged.
Being forgotten in return for forgetting the signs gives a reciprocal consequence, but not the focal punishment formula.
Faces are humbled before the Living Sustainer and the bearer of wrongdoing fails, closely supporting humiliation at judgment.
Temporary mercy and enjoyment do not clarify the focus.
The gift of a book for guidance does not add to the punishment warning.
Brief enjoyment followed by painful punishment supplies a compressed consequence pattern.
The creation and lordship argument does not clarify the punishment, humiliation, or abiding outcome.
The deniers demand that God's punishment be brought, directly invoking its arrival as a challenge.
It directly assigns hypocrites a painful punishment, though without the focus's humiliation and permanence.
The water and vegetation cycle does not clarify the focal judgment formula.
Its warning of severe requital is secondary to a ritual legal instruction.
The criminal who comes to the Lord enters Hell where neither death nor life ends the condition.
The same-surah fire above and below depicts an enclosing punitive environment and explicitly functions as warning.
The request for angels to come concerns proof, not the punishment that comes in the focus.
It directly declares the Lord's punishment inevitable.
The immediately nearby assertion that none can guide whom God misguides reinforces the warning's decisive authority.
Treasures and an honorable station do not clarify punishment arriving or settling.
Noah is sent to warn his people before a painful punishment comes to them.
The immediately preceding allocation of guidance and misguidance to each self frames the personal consequence in the focus.
It directly contrasts worldly humiliation with the greater punishment of the Hereafter in the same surah.
Reverent fear of the Lord's punishment supports its seriousness, without describing its arrival or duration.
The same-surah declaration of God as creator and guardian of all things grounds His authority over the consequence.
It explicitly calls the Fire an evil settled and abiding place.
It directly names humiliating punishment in this life, a more humiliating afterlife punishment, and absence of help.
The same-surah statement of God's control of the heavens and earth frames the loss of those who reject His signs.
Its good abiding abode is a contrary parallel that clarifies the focus's lasting punitive residence.
Fruit and palm sheaths do not clarify the focal warning.
The question about whether a report has come offers only a formal echo of arrival.
The prayer for a teaching messenger does not illuminate punishment, humiliation, or endurance.
Receiving the record in the left hand begins the adverse final outcome, though the focal formula is not stated.
The decree falling upon deniers gives a limited parallel to punishment settling upon them.
The report of Abraham's honored guests does not clarify the focus.
Rescue from great distress is not tied to the focal punishment sequence.
The repeated rejection of messengers does not itself describe punishment, humiliation, or permanence.
Household etiquette does not clarify the focus.
Continuing doubt ends when the Hour or an irreversible day's punishment comes suddenly.
It joins the Fire as an enduring destination with divine wrath, curse, and a great punishment.
It states that deniers are companions of the Fire, abiding there.
The angels' punishment at death includes the command to taste the burning punishment.
It declares Hell already encompassing the disbelievers.
It names painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter for those who turn away.
It presents repeated punishment followed by return to a great punishment.
It explicitly calls the requital for wrongdoing the punishment of eternity.
It warns of an overwhelming punishment from God coming upon people or the Hour arriving suddenly.
It contrasts worldly punishment with the more severe punishment of the Hereafter.
It assigns one who seeks only the immediate world to Hell, entering it blamed and banished.
It depicts a Fire enclosing wrongdoers and an unbearable punishment within it.
Turning from the Reminder results in bearing a burden on the Day of Resurrection.
It calls that burden abiding and an evil burden on the Day of Resurrection.
The Fire comes upon disbelievers suddenly, leaving them unable to repel it or receive help.
Even a slight touch of the Lord's punishment makes wrongdoers acknowledge their wrongdoing.
It depicts garments of Fire and boiling liquid poured over those who disbelieve.
It explicitly assigns those who disbelieve in God's signs a humiliating punishment.
Seizing the prosperous with punishment turns their denial into helpless outcry.
It calls the punishment of Hell an inescapably clinging punishment.
Deniers do not believe until they see the painful punishment.
The painful punishment comes upon them suddenly while they are unaware.
It assigns those who disbelieve in the Hereafter the worst punishment.
Those who bring evil are cast face-first into the Fire as requital.
It declares Hell encompassing the disbelievers, despite their demand to hasten punishment.
It declares that Hell will be filled with jinn and people who reject faith.
Those bound for the Fire are returned to it whenever they try to leave and told to taste its punishment.
It declares that God has cursed the disbelievers and prepared a blazing Fire for them.
It explicitly says they will abide in that Fire forever without protector or helper.
It attributes to those who deny the Hereafter a punishment of painful torment.
It portrays the Fire of Hell as a condition neither ended by death nor lightened.
The speaker fears the punishment of a tremendous Day for disobeying the Lord.
It depicts a wrongdoer warding off the evil punishment with his face on the Day of Resurrection.
It describes wrongdoers seeking to ransom themselves from the evil punishment on the Day of Resurrection.
It warns to turn in submission before punishment comes, when help will no longer be available.
It depicts the shame of those who lied about God on the Day of Resurrection.
It shows the disbelievers driven in groups toward Hell after the warning has come to them.
It commands entry through the gates of Hell to abide there, calling it an evil abode for the arrogant.
It depicts the people of Pharaoh exposed to the Fire and then commanded into the severest punishment.
It names a humiliating thunderbolt punishment that seized those who rejected guidance.
It explicitly describes criminals abiding in the punishment of Hell.
It joins scalding liquid with burning in Hell for the denier who has gone astray.
It assigns those who disbelieve in their Lord the punishment of Hell and calls it an evil destination.
It begins the final command to seize and cast the condemned person into Hell.
It identifies Hell as the blazing fire that strips away what it reaches.
It declares Hell to be lying in wait for transgressors.
It describes transgressors remaining in Hell for long periods.
It assigns disbelievers the Fire of Hell, abiding there permanently.
